newsitem.title: USA: Scientists see how antioxidants may fight cancer.
newsitem.headline: Scientists see how antioxidants may fight cancer.

text.p: Scientists say they may have found at least part of the reason why green vegetables containing antioxidants appear to fight cancer.

Oxidants are oxygen-containing molecules called free radicals. Many scientists believe they can damage DNA and the membrane of cells in ways that lead to cancer, but a report in Friday's edition of the journal Science adds a new dimension.

Researchers from Johns Hopkins in Baltimore suggest that cancer cells themselves may cause a surplus of oxidants, which send signals that promote yet more uncontrolled cell growth. Antioxidants that interfere with these protein signals may block the process, they said.
"Control of signaling pathways involving oxidants may explain why some antioxidants appear to prevent development of certain cancers," Hopkins cardiologist Kaikobad Irani said.
The scientists studied connective tissue cells that produce a cancer-causing gene called H-RasV12. They also studied non-cancerous cells.

The cancer cells produced larger amounts of an oxidant called superoxide O2. But it could be blocked in several ways -- by cells carrying certain genes, known as Ras or Rac1, by treatment with two protein inhibitors, and, most importantly, by treatment with an antioxidant called N-acetyl-L-cysteine.

"Our results should help researchers understand important biochemical pathways in cancer and contribute to the future development of treatment strategies," said Dr. Pascal Goldschmidt-Clermont, who did the research at Hopkins but is now at Ohio State University.
